newsitem.title: USA: Soybeans hit eight-year high, coffee stalls.
newsitem.headline: Soybeans hit eight-year high, coffee stalls.

text.p: Soybean prices soared to their highest level for more than eight years Friday amid concern about rapidly disappearing supplies in the United States.
Analysts said prices would have to rise further to ration demand, with stocks at the end of the current season on August 31 already projected at the lowest in two decades.
"The reduction in usage still is not severe enough," said Bob Lekberg, an analyst with Goldenberg-Hehmeyer. "That's finally what the market is coming around to realizing."
The U.S. Agriculture Department last month estimated stocks at the end of the current marketing year (1996/97) at 125 million bushels.
"The cutback in usage in the last half of the year will have to be at record severity to keep that carry (ending stocks) at 125 (million bushels)," Lekberg said.
He said stocks could be "getting down close to zero (bushels) by early harvest." Farmers in the U.S. Midwest usually begin cutting early maturing varieties in September.

On the Chicago Board of Trade soybeans for May delivery rose to a peak of $8.98-1/2 a bushel, the highest level for the nearby contract since August 1988. Some profit taking emerged late and May closed up 7-1/4 cents at $8.87-1/2.
Coffee prices tumbled on Friday, erasing some of sharp gains seen earlier in the week, although some traders viewed the fall as a short-term setback in a bull market.

"The market may deserve to go a bit lower, but overall the fundamentals have not changed," said Smith Barney analyst Walt Spilka. "The bottom line is, the season is over for most producing countries, they've sold out almost everything and there's not a lot of coffee around."
Prices had surged 30 cents per pound, or 15 percent, in the four previous sessions and started the day higher before speculative profit taking turned the market around.
At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, coffee for May delivery closed at 247.55 cents a pound, down 5.20 cents on the day.
Gasoline prices fell sharply on the New York Mercantile Exchange after weak crude prices in the last two sessions finally forced funds to take profits in gasoline which had so far bucked declines.
Gasoline for June delivery finished 2.11 cents lower at 60.52 cents a gallon. June crude ended 31 cents a barrel lower at $19.60 while June heating oil fell 1.31 cents a gallon to 53.02 cents.
"We are back on the defensive again," said Tom Bentz, analyst with ING Derivatives in New York.
"Gasoline had been holding up while everything else broke down," Bentz said.

Dealers said crude's weakness reflects rising supplies in the U.S. Gulf Coast, the site of highest demand due to the concentration of refineries in the area. Meanwhile, heating oil is seasonally out of favor.
Dealers said gasoline should hold the 60.00 cent level in the near term as it represents good value amid the seasonally strongest period for demand.
"Sixty cent gasoline in June is pretty good value since that is after Memorial Day weekend," said a dealer, noting a popular driving holiday.
